assignmentHtml.task: Audit claims G1 and G2 about Stardust. Starting point: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/stardust/. Key questions: (1) Did Stardust return comet Wild 2 material in January 2006? (2) Was there a lander that touched down and drilled? (3) What glycine findings were reported from returned material? (4) How was extraterrestrial origin distinguished from terrestrial contamination? (5) Did glycine detection establish living organisms or a complete protein? Find the original papers, NASA releases, and discussion of glycine provenance controversy.
assignmentHtml.context: Mission: Stardust (comet sample return). Target: comet 81P/Wild 2. Claims G1-G2: G1 says Stardust returned Wild 2 material in Jan 2006 and involved a lander touching down and drilling. G2 says glycine was a building block used by life, and distinguishing extraterrestrial origin from contamination required evidence, and detecting glycine alone established neither life nor complete proteins. These are claims to audit.
assignmentHtml.expected_output: Verdict on each component of G1 and G2 with corrected text, dates, source URLs. Clarify: capsule vs lander, exact return date, glycine findings and their provenance debate, contamination controls.

answerHtml: G1 partially correct: Stardust did return Wild 2 material on January 15, 2006 via a Sample Return Capsule (SRC), but there was NO lander and NO drilling — Stardust was a flyby spacecraft that collected dust in aerogel panels as it passed through the comet's coma at ~150 km distance. G2 is fully correct: glycine (a single amino acid, one of 20 proteinogenic building blocks of proteins) was detected; its extraterrestrial origin required isotopic evidence (δ13C = +29 ± 6‰, far outside the terrestrial range of −6 to −40‰); and detection of glycine alone established neither life nor any complete protein or even a peptide.

evidence.snippet: NASA's Stardust was the first spacecraft to bring samples from a comet to Earth... Mission Type: Flyby, Sample Return. The samples were to be collected using a low-density microporous silica-based substance known as aerogel, attached to panels on the spacecraft to 'soft-catch' and preserve the cometary materials. At 05:57 UT Jan. 15, 2006, Stardust's Sample Return Capsule (SRC) separated from the main vehicle and four hours later entered Earth's atmosphere. Slowed by parachutes, the capsule landed at 10:10 UT within a 19×52-mile landing zone at the U.S. Air Force Test and Training Range in Utah.
evidence.supports: Stardust was a flyby/sample-return mission (NOT a lander); SRC returned January 15, 2006; collection was via aerogel panels, not drilling

evidence.snippet: Stardust was a 385-kilogram robotic space probe... Its primary mission was to collect dust samples from the coma of comet Wild 2... Mission type: Sample return. Cometary and interstellar particles are collected in ultra low density aerogel. The tennis racket-sized collector tray contained ninety blocks of aerogel... The particle collector uses aerogel, a low-density, inert, microporous, silica-based substance, to capture dust grains as the spacecraft passes through the coma of Wild 2.
evidence.supports: Confirms flyby/sample-return design, aerogel collection, no lander component anywhere in the mission architecture

evidence.snippet: The δ13C value for glycine of +29 ± 6‰ strongly suggests an extraterrestrial origin for glycine, while the δ13C value for EACA of −25 ± 2‰ indicates terrestrial contamination by Nylon-6 during curation. This represents the first compound-specific isotopic analysis of a cometary organic compound. ... The measured δ13C value for glycine falls well outside the terrestrial range for organic carbon of −6‰ to −40‰. ... Our analysis also reveals contamination of Stardust cometary collector foils from the Nylon-6 storage and shipping bags used during curation. ... We spent two years testing and developing our equipment... procedural blanks included commercial aluminum foil heated at 500°C; all glassware was also heated at 500°C.
evidence.supports: Glycine detected in Wild 2 foils; extraterrestrial origin established via compound-specific carbon isotope ratio (+29±6‰ vs terrestrial −6 to −40‰); contamination controls documented (heated blanks, isotopic comparison with Nylon-6 bags); glycine existed as both free form (~40%) and bound precursors liberated by acid hydrolysis

evidence.snippet: Sandford et al. 2010, 'Assessment and control of organic contaminants': Glycine was found in SRC SLA backshell (770 nmol/g) and PICA heatshield (189 nmol/g) at high levels — potential contamination sources. The carbon isotopic ratio of EACA matched Nylon-6 storage bags (δ13C = −25±2‰ for Stardust foils vs −26.8±0.2‰ for JSC bag), confirming terrestrial origin of that contaminant. D-amino acids present in UTTR soil but NOT in flight witness tile, providing evidence that landing-site soil contamination did not significantly affect the comet-exposed samples.
evidence.supports: Comprehensive contamination assessment; multiple terrestrial sources identified and characterized; landing site contamination ruled out for flight foils via D-amino acid evidence

evidence.snippet: Hints of the simplest amino acid, glycine, were found in samples returned to Earth in 2006 from Comet Wild-2 by NASA's Stardust mission. However, possible terrestrial contamination of the dust samples made the analysis extremely difficult. ... 'This is the first unambiguous detection of glycine at a comet,' says Kathrin Altwegg, principal investigator of the ROSINA instrument.
evidence.supports: ESA acknowledges the Stardust glycine finding was NOT unambiguous due to contamination concerns; contrasts with Rosetta's direct detection as the first 'unambiguous' one

evidence.snippet: As one of the 20 proteinogenic amino acids, glycine is a fundamental building block of proteins in all life... The principal function of glycine is it acts as a precursor to proteins. Most proteins incorporate only small quantities of glycine... Glycine is not strictly essential to the human diet, as it is biosynthesized in the body.
evidence.supports: Glycine is a single amino acid building block of proteins — NOT life itself, NOT a complete protein, NOT a peptide; detection of a single amino acid does not establish living organisms

evidence.snippet: 'Glycine is an amino acid used by living organisms to make proteins, and this is the first time an amino acid has been found in a comet,' said Jamie Elsila. ... 'We discovered that the Stardust-returned glycine has an extraterrestrial carbon isotope signature, indicating that it originated on the comet.' ... Earlier, preliminary analysis detected glycine in both the foil and aerogel. However, since glycine is used by terrestrial life, at first the team was unable to rule out contamination from sources on Earth.
evidence.supports: NASA's own announcement confirms: (a) glycine is a building block of proteins (not life itself); (b) isotopic analysis was required to distinguish extraterrestrial from terrestrial glycine; (c) initial detection could not rule out contamination without isotopic evidence
